utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution is now prepared for its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you kind enough to read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, since you and I speak the same language, I would just remind you that we need to speak a little slowly that so the interpreter can keep pace. And for the similar -- or actually for the same reason, if you could permit a brief pause between my question and your answer and I will do the same after every answer before going on to the next question. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges your full name.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Peter Norbert Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I was born on 14th July, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And were was that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: In Louvain, Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What languages to you speak?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Flemish, French and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a little bit now about your background. Could you please tell us about your education first.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah I graduated from the University of California at Santa Barbara in 1993 withe a degree in law and society and African studies. Then I went on to law school at Stanford law school, where I graduated with a juris doctor degree, JD, in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a little bit about now about work experience. Can you tell us what you did after law school for your first work experience.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: During law school I took a year off to work at a legal resources centre, constitutional litigation unit in Johannesburg. After law school I immediately went to work at Human Rights Watch first as a fellow, then as a researcher and presently as a senior researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What year was that when you first went to Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was in 1997, September, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you told us that you first went there as a fellow. How long were you a fellow at Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I was a fellow for a period of one year in the Africa division.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did that fellowship have a name?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It was called the Orville Schell Fellowship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: During that career, of your fellowship when in the Africas Division what sort of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I first went to South Africa to do research on South Africa's treatment of undocumented migrants and asylum seekers, which was published later as a report called "Prohibited Persons." I also went to Uganda to do research on the political system in Uganda as well as the war in northern Uganda with the Lord's Resistance Army and in western Uganda with the Allied Democratic Forces, which resulted in the publication of a report called "Hostile to Democracy."

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. Perhaps because we're both speaking the same language both Prosecution and the witness, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You could only have said that with Mr. Guy-Smith absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I think for the interpretation I'd ask my learned friend and witness perhaps to pause slightly between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Khan. And no doubt all counsel will take note of that as the matter progress. Mr. Shin, things are running a little quick for the people to keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have apparently already violated my own caution to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Khan will act as your conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, as you probably heard, we have both probably prompted first by me started speaking a little bit too quickly. So I will be mindful of that and will ask that you be as well.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We had left off your speaking about your fellowship. You told us earlier that following your fellowship you continued on at HRW. Could you tell us what you did next after your fellowship, what you did at Human Rights Watch. I'm sorry, could you tell us what position you held and then tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Just before the completion of my fellowship in late July 1998 I was approached by the Europe and Central Asia Division of Human Rights Watch to join our work on Kosovo and I became researcher in September 1998 after the completion of my fellowship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How long did you work as a researcher at Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I worked as a researcher at Human Rights Watch till December 1999 when I became a senior searcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just to stay right now with the names of the positions that you held. How long have you been a senior searcher?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Since December 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And does that mean that you are still a senior researcher now?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is there a particular part of Human Rights Watch within which you work?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I head our Emergencies Unit which focuses on research in war zones around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Before I ask you further about the Emergencies Unit, if you could take you back to when you began your work in Kosovo. You said that you were first approached shortly before July of 1998 about working on Kosovo and then became a researcher in, I believe you said September of that year. Could you tell us what you did in between the time that you were first -- you first started working on Kosovo and when you became a researcher if that was different from what you were doing as a researcher.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: My work as a fellow also was a research-like job. It was just a special entry-position programme. We had a Human Rights Watch for people who wanted to come and become researchers at Human Rights Watch. So my work as a fellow and as a researcher was similar in content.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, as a researcher on Kosovo, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: As soon as I was asked to join the work on Kosovo in late July 1998, I began to work very closely with our then senior researcher on Kosovo, Fred Abrahams, who had been working in the Balkans for many years. And our immediate -- my immediate work involved my own preparation for a mission we would undertake in September 1998 to Kosovo, as well as supporting Fred in the preparation of a report he was finalising based on several research trips he made to Kosovo called "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you more about your work in Kosovo shortly, but before we do that if I could just ask you a little bit more about your other work with Human Rights Watch. Just remind us: Approximately how long have you been with the Emergencies Units within Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, the Emergencies Unit was formed in December 1999 and I was the first person in that unit, and have been the head of the unit up to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is the Emergency Unit? Could you describe that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch is an international human rights organisation and we have a special expertise in doing research in conflict-related area. The Emergency Unit at Human Rights Watch serves as a repository for that experience, both in terms of kind of the security challenges we face working in conflicts zones as well as our IHL, international humanitarian law experience. So whenever a major conflict like Iraq, Afghanistan, Chechnya or Kosovo breaks out, it's the Emergencies Unit which is the working with the divisional regional researchers who sets up a response and who are often the first people on the ground to document violation of the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've mentioned Iraq and Afghanistan. Are there other places within which you worked as a researcher for the Emergencies Unit?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. There's countries all around the world. Would you like me to name them?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You needn't name all of them but if give us some more examples of places where you have done work as a researcher.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It would include Sierra Leone; the Democratic Republic of Congo; Uganda, in Africa; Kosovo and Macedonia in the Balkans; Chechnya; Afghanistan; Iraq; Israel and the occupied territories; southern Thailand, Nepal, Azerbaijan and some other countries which I can't recall right now. There's about a dozen countries on which I have written reports for Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And approximately how many reports have you written for Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I think at last count there was 23 or 24 reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Have you produced documents other than reports?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. The reports are books or shorter stapled reports but there's also shorter work, materials such as press releases. I would estimate there was at least over hundred press releases. OpEd editorials in major newspapers like The New York Times and the Washington Post, International Herald Tribune, and some European papers; letters to governments and international organisations; various advocacy materials as well as a few academic articles relating to the democratic process in South Africa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, have you testified previously on the basis or on the basis of work that you have done from Human Rights Watch or for reasons otherwise arising from work you have done in Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I have not testified before a court or a tribunal. But I have provided testimony in front of the Foreign Relations Committee in United States Senate about war crimes in Chechnya as well in front of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. The Political Affairs Committee of the Parliamentary Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: From all of this work that have you done in the human rights area do you also give talks on it or attend conferences?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us where and on what topics.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I have spoken at the Pearson Peacekeeping Institute about the role of human rights in peacekeeping exercises. That talk was particularly focussed on our experiences in Kosovo. I have also given talks about my work at various law schools, including repeatedly at Stanford Law School, my alma mater at UC Berkeley, and at Columbia University.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've mentioned that one topic that you have mentioned is your experience in Kosovo. Could you just give us a general idea of what -- what other topics, if there indeed others, that you have given talks on.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Most of my talks were explanatory talks about the nature of the work and how we conducted the work. So it focussed on approach to our research, how we did our field work and wrote up our field work as well as the sources of law that we use in our work including various human rights instruments as well as the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert have you ever received any honours for the work that you have done in human rights?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I have received a few honours. I was elected as a term member to the Council on Foreign Relations, which is a policy body in the United States. I also was recognised as the public-interest lawyer of the year by Stanford Law School and -- at the same year, and this was last year, I was recognised by the human rights community in Azerbaijan as their human rights lawyer of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'm actually listening to the French translation to maybe sure we don't get too far ahead of the interpreters. I'd like to ask you now, moving to Human Rights Watch, I'd like to ask you a little bit about that organisation. What is Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch is one of the two largest international human rights organisations, an honour we share with Amnesty International. We're an independent non-governmental organisation which does research, writes about and does advocacy to promote human rights and adherence to the laws of war around the world. We're an organisation of about 200 people at the moment. We've been growing quite fast and we work in about 80 countries around the world. My programme has a special expertise in the laws of war and documenting violations in conflicts areas, but our work spans a very wide range of topics from conflict-related issues to protecting the rights of people with HIV/AIDS, just to give one example. Most of our reports -- all of our reports are public. They're widely distributed to policy-makers and various international bodies and they're also available on our wet site. We also engage in a wide range of advocacy activities: Supporting the formation of the International Criminal Court; we're a founding member of the international campaign to ban the use of land-mines; the international campaign to stop the use of child soldiers; just to give a few examples. We do not accept any money from any government. All of our funding is privately raised to ensure our independence and objectivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where is Human Rights Watch based?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Our headquarters are in New York City but we have satellite offices around the world, in Brussels, London, Washington D.C., Moscow, and some smaller field offices in other places because we truly consider ourselves a global human rights organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Does HRW, being based in New York, does it investigate alleged human rights abuses in the United States or the other countries within which it has offices?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We document -- we have a very active programme which has certainly become more actively since the events of 9/11 on documenting human rights violations in the United States. We also document abuses committed by U.S. forces deployed in places like Iraq and Afghanistan which has been part of my work as well. And we investigate abuses in all of the countries that we have offices in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned investigations a few times so this may be part of your answer to my next question. How does Human Rights Watch go about doing it's work?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, unlike a lot of more policy-oriented organisations, the strength of Human Rights Watch is that we go out and investigate abuses committed in the field themselves. We travel to the countries that we're researching. We meet with victims and witnesses to abuses as well as local and national officials. So our reports are based on primary investigations from wide range of sources. Our public reports are heavily footnoted to ensure that the readers of those reports know where our office information is coming from. So in addition to the careful editing of our reports, they can assess for themselves the reliability of our information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you have begun explaining to us a little bit the way in which Human Rights Watch goes about doing its investigation. Could you tell us how is a report prepared and the relationship between that and the investigations as you have outlined it for us.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: In most of the countries we work in, we have had a long-standing research programme in that country. For example, we started our work in Kosovo in 1990. So we have access to a very extensive source -- sources of information ranging from the diplomatic to local and international correspondents, to victim and witnesses, hospital workers. Really a very broad range of information. Normally we would be in the field gathering information on specific topics for a period of two weeks anywhere up to two, three months, conducting interviews. Then we go home. We collate that information into a report format to assess the reliability of witness statements try to corroborate various accounts. We exclude quite a significant amount of the information that we have gathered, because we feel it's not reliable enough not to be made public. Then we make a draft report, which is written up by the researchers who conducted the field work, people like myself, which is then reviewed by our legal office, our office of counsel, which consists of people with significant experience and legal backgrounds. They review the report and send queries to us and ultimately proof the report. Then it goes to our programme division who review the report again. Sorry. I forgot one step. Prior to the report going to counsel, it's reviewed by the regional division. So in the case of Kosovo, that would be the Europe and Central Asia Division. Then goes to counsel, then programme division, which ensures that our findings and our recommendations are consistent throughout the organisation and who also check for accuracy. In the case of particularly sensitive reports which includes the reports on Kosovo, because of the prominence of our work on Kosovo, those reports would also bb reviewed by executive director prior to publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could ask you a few questions about the procedure you have just outlined for us now. You have mentioned I think the counsel's office, the programme division and regional divisions. Just so that we're clear, these are all parts of Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now the procedure that you have outlined as well, in your experience was that a procedure generally approached -- applied at Human Rights Watch? Or maybe I should put it this way: How generally was that applied?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: All of our reports are reviewed in this careful manner, because -- the reason why we are well known and effective human rights Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. organisation is because of the reliability of our reports. And making errors in our reports will have a devastating impact on our ability to influence policy-makers. So this very extensive review process is used for all reports. Obviously, as I pointed out, in the case of Kosovo and other particularly high-profile work of the organisation, another example would be our work on the Israeli defence forces operation in Jenin. The executive director and other senior management people would also become directly involved in reviewing our research and our recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You have told us there are a wide range of sources from which Human Rights Watch receives information or gathers information. Could you explain to us how Human Rights Watch assesses those sources.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We receive information which ranges from rumours to very detailed accounts by direct eyewitnesses. We try to corroborate information as much as possible, preferably through going and investigating in situ where events have occurred and tracking down direct witnesses. We interview witnesses and victims in private; we interview them separately from each other and take detailed statements which allow us to cross-corroborate information. When we're dealing with information which does in the come from eyewitnesses or victims, such as reports from other human rights organisations or from journalists, normally we would be familiar with the work methodology of those journalists or local human rights organisations or international groups like the International Committee of the Red Cross, which would allow us to assess that kind of secondary-source information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, receiving this range of information that you have told us about and the value of being accurate which you have also mentioned, has Human Rights Watch ever declined to publish a report or any other document based on the information it has received?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes on any mission we go to we exclude a significant amount of information from our reports that we have received, either because we consider it to be unreliable or because we have been unable to substantiate those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say unreliable, how do you determine whether something is unreliable or not?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well it will again depend on our knowledge of the source, our familiarity with the work methodology of the source and whether or not we have received any other information which is consistent or inconsistent with that information. Whenever we receive secondary information from any source our first attempt will be to seek primary substantiation of that information by going to track down the witnesses or victims ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend. I've just consulted with both of my colleagues on this side of the bench. I can say as far as the Defence is concerned, there is no dispute that Human Rights Watch is a reputable international organisation and that generally the reports are fair and accurate. If that helps my learned friend move things on a little faster, then that is our hope and intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Powles and your colleagues. You heard that, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes very grateful move on directly to the next topic. And the next topic, Mr. Bouckaert, will be this: What does Human Rights Watch do after a report is published?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We're in the business of promoting and protecting -- promoting human rights and protecting people from human rights violations. So after the publication of a report we would normally engage in a vigorous advocacy campaign, both with the national authorities and with the international authorities to try to stop the abuses and also to seek accountability, if necessary, for abuses that we have documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We made address this issue of the advocacy that you are talking about again later. Right now, if I could direct your attention to the work that Human Rights Watch has done in Kosovo. Are you familiar with the work the Human Rights Watch did in Kosovo before you joined Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. And I reviewed that material in my preparation before going to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When did Human Rights Watch first begin doing work in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch was formed as Helsinki Watch in 1978 and has had an extensive focus on eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. Our work in Kosovo intensified after 1989 [Realtime transcript read in error: "1999"] when Slobodan Milosevic withdrew the autonomy of Kosovo and human rights abuses in Kosovo increased and against a majority ethnic Albanian population increased exponentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The transcript says that the -- your work in Kosovo became intensive in 1989 when Milosevic withdrew the human rights; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Between this time when the work became a little more intensive in 1989 and the time that you joined Human Rights Watch, how many reports did Human Rights Watch publish on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of armed conflict in Kosovo, we published at least four major reports that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And could you just give us a month and date and time range? We're talking from about 1989 to when?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: 1989, 1990. I'm not sure when first report was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, following from Mr. Powles' comments, these reports are in the public domain. There's no objection to my friend leading on the dates it assists the witness. THE COURT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Once again, I'm very grateful to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think the general mood is one that you can anticipate a general level of acceptance about the background material and lead fairly swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert if you could just tell us briefly, then, what sorts of abuses were covered by those reports?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They dealt with -- the four reports that we issued dealt with very similar abuses. After Milosevic came to power, in the then Yugoslavia, he withdraw the autonomy of Kosovo. The public service and universities, hospitals and other various sectors of society were purged of Albanian official. There was a vast level of police abuse, unfair trials and other such abuses conduct the against the ethnic Albanian majority of Kosovo. The ethnic Albanian population of Kosovo responded with relatively peaceful protests under the control and authority of president Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think that should suffice to explain types of abused that you were dealing with. I would like to turn to the work that you were doing in Kosovo and the reports that you were produced during the time that you were doing that work. And if we could begin with -- with the people who did that work. Who from Human Rights Watch apart from yourself was doing work on Kosovo when you were working on it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: In terms of the research, the research staff included Fred Abrahams, our senior researcher working on Kosovo as well as Albania and Macedonia and Serbia, although during the period of the conflict his work was almost exclusively on Kosovo; as well as myself and a number of short-term consultants we hired to cover specific aspects of the conflict. Later on, as the conflict became more intensified and ultimately led to the NATO war in Kosovo, an additional number of people were hired by Human Rights Watch and research staff from other parts of the Balkans were reassigned to working on the Kosovo conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what kind of presence did Human Rights Watch have on the ground from -- let's say, first, let me ask you first. Do you know when Fred Abrahams started working on Kosovo? Just the time period.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he started working on Kosovo. He covered Kosovo as part of his work in the Balkans since the early 1990s when he joined the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What kind of presence in Kosovo did Human Rights Watch have from the time that you joined? And you explained that was I think about July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. When I joined, Fred Abrahams had just returned from -- what I believe was his second research trip to Kosovo since the outbreak the intensification of armed conflict in Kosovo in about late February 1998. Then Fred and I started planning for a research trip to Kosovo which took place in September 1998 and we returned again in November 1998. At that time, access to Kosovo was very difficult because of the obstacles we faced from the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This time period, you mention February 1998 to November 1998. What kind of presence on the ground did Human Rights Watch have?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: As I explained, I personally took part in those two research trips which both took place over -- we were in country for a period of about three weeks each time. And Fred had made two similar research trips earlier in the year. So from February to November 1998, we had been to Kosovo four times, each time for a period much about three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did Human Rights Watch do its work during this time period, the time period that you were involved? Did it do its work on its own or did it have any involvement with others?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Kosovo certainly had much less of an international presence during the conflict in 1998 than it does today. We did consult closely with Amnesty International who were also travelling to the region. And we worked particularly closely with the Humanitarian Law Centre, a Belgrade-based human rights organisation of great repute, as well as the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms which was an ethnic Albanian-dominated human rights organisation based in Kosovo. And we obviously had very regular contacts with various diplomatic officials who were based in Kosovo: the International Committee of the Red Cross; the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, which was in Kosovo at the time; various international journalists and local journalists, particularly the journalists at the ethnic Albanian newspaper Koha Ditore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just briefly on two organisations. The Humanitarian Law Centre that you have described as a human rights organisation, where was that based first?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The Humanitarian Law Centre was a Belgrade-based -- was and is, I should say, a Belgrade-based human rights organisation headed by Natasa Kandic. It has worked throughout the Balkans and played a very courageous and independent role in documenting the abuses committed in Bosnia, Croatia as well as Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. If I just interrupt you to a couple of follow-up questions. Did you know the people for that organisation who worked in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: There was one Serbian woman, her name was Gordana, as well as four or five ethnic Albanians whose names I cannot remember at this stage. It's been quite a while. As well as Natasa Kandic herself, who came down quite regularly to work with the team and to review their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know how they did their work?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We frequently went on field visits ourselves to investigate abuses and met every few days when we were in the country, both in Kosovo and Belgrade to discuss the findings, the things that we were finding, what kind of investigations we hoped to carry out as well as the difficulties that we were facing. And we were so impressed with their methodology which very closely mirrored our own that we actually ended up hiring two of their staff to come work for Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning now to the reports that were produced during your time. Could you tell us just the title. What was the first -- what was the first -- what was the title of the first Human Rights Watch report that was published while you were working on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: When I joined, Fred Abrahams was completing a report called "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo." It was completed in late October 1998, completed and released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just the time period. What time period was addressed by that book?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The time period addressed in the book starts in late February 1998, when a series of very severe attacks by Yugoslavia and Serbian forces took place in the Decan area -- sorry, the Drenica area of Kosovo and ends in -- up to late September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear. Could you explain to us what specifically your role was in the preparation of this book for publishing?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. There was a period of just more than a month prior to us travelling to Kosovo, and that would be August 1998, in which I helped Fred Abrahams finalise the text of the report, and we continued to finalise and update the text of the report up to and including information from our September 1998 visit to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How familiar are you with the contents of that report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: At the time I could have recited it in my sleep because we worked on it for such a long time, every day arguing over what cases to include, what information we had. So I was very familiar with the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know the methodology that Human Rights Watch used in this particular report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how does that compare to the methodology that you have described earlier for Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We used the same methodology in that report that we normally use. There were some great difficulties in reaching some places in Kosovo because of the ongoing conflict and the hostile position of the Yugoslavia government towards our work in Kosovo. But the methodology was essentially the same as I have described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We'll get to some of those points shortly. Could you just provide very briefly a summary of what those findings in the report are. You have told us and let me just say that you did tell us that the book addressed a series of very severe attacks in the Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult to summarise a report of over 100 pages in just a few words. Basically, the report deals with the abuses committed by both the Yugoslav and Serbian forces in Kosovo, as well as the UCK, what you say, the Kosovo Liberation Army during this period of time. We found that the Yugoslavia forces and Serbian forces had committed the majority of the violations during that time and those were massive an amounted to war crimes. They included widespread summary executions of civilians; attacks on civilian targets; shelling of civilian targets; the use of the Red Cross emblem during attacks, attacks -- arbitrary arrests and torture and killings in detention. I think that gives a pretty good idea of what we were finding on the Yugoslav side. In terms of the KLA side, we found that there had been a significant number of abductions of some ethnic Serbs and ethnic Albanian and some Roma during this period of time which we estimated to be at least over 100 persons and some of those persons had been found dead after last being seen in KLA custody. The report also has an extensive analysis of the legal nature of the conflict in Kosovo and the applicability of Common Article 3 and the Protocol Additional to the Geneva Conventions to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, if you can say how would -- and you would also feel free to tell us if it's not possible to say -- how would the abuses you investigated or that Human Rights Watch investigated alleged to have been committed by the KLA compared to the abuses alleged to have been committed by Yugoslav and Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We don't necessarily like to engage to that kind of comparative analysis, but certainly, during this period of the conflict in Kosovo the vast majority of the abuses committed in the conflict were committed by the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning to this area where abuses alleged to have been committed by the KLA. What were the sources that Human Rights Watch had for these alleged abuses?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was very difficult for us to track down direct eyewitnesses and victims. Too many of the abductions and killings committed by the KLA, we certainly tried to and sought the cooperation of the Yugoslav government in both tracking down witnesses and gaining access to autopsies conducted on bodies that the Yugoslav government claimed to have found. But we found no cooperation from the Yugoslav authorities at this stage. We were able to confirm some of these abductions through primary sources, particularly the abductions of -- two separate abductions involving two Serbian journalists each time. But for most of the cases we had to reply on information provided to us by the previously mentioned Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade; the International Committee of the Red Cross; some journalistic sources, as well information provided to us by the Yugoslav and Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've told us about difficulty in cooperation from Yugoslavia -- from the Yugoslavian government. Were there other difficulties that Human Rights Watch encountered in trying to investigate abused alleged to have been committed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it was difficult to find Serbian translators who were willing to travel through KLA-held territory into Serbian villages to speak to witnesses there. They were concerned about their own safety and in most cases the Serbs in those villages refused to talk to Albanian translators because they believed that the Albanian translators were not translating the information accurately. In many cases, when went to Serbian villages we also faced personal threats and hostility to our own safety. Many Serbs in Kosovo believed the kind of propaganda President Slobodan Milosevic was spreading and his government was spreading about the role of international organisations in Kosovo. So they saw us as the enemy. So unfortunately, even though we were deeply concerned about these victims, it was often very difficult to get to speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And those were the problems in going to Serbian villages. Any problem with going to Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: An additional factor is a that many people in KLA-held territory simply were too afraid to talk about those kind of abuses because they faced -- they were concerned about probable or possible retaliation by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the KLA. So people were much more unwilling to speak about abuses by the KLA in KLA-held territory than they were willing to speak about abused by the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, with the assistance of the usher I would like to show you a document and this will be tab 5 in the bundle which has been provided. Mr. Bouckaert, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This is a report that I have been speaking about. It's our report called "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo," which we released in late October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, going to the issue about abuses allegedly committed by the KLA, is there is a particular report that addresses that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that is Chapter 10, which -- yes, which starts on page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for the record that is -- that page ERN K0364865. And this is the first time for me, but I will attempt to do this in Sanction as well to make it easier to follow the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert -- sorry, just one moment, please. I'd like to direct your attention to page 78 of that report which bears the ERN number K0364868 and in particular to go -- there's a heading in the middle of the page "Abduction of Ethnic Serbs." Now before we address that tell us again: In the area of abductions what numbers are we talking about? What numbers did Human Rights Watch find?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: In terms of abductions by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We found that the most reliable estimates ranged somewhere between 100 and 140 persons being abducted by the KLA. There were some higher figures provided by the Yugoslav authorities and those we considered a little bit less reliable. And they also included people who had been abducted by the KLA for short periods of time. So the number of 100 to 140 reflects the number of people who were actually abducted and still missing at the time of the publication of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for the time when these abductions took place, what time period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We're talking basically from late February 1998 up to the publication of the report. The figures cited in the report mostly date from around August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And geographically, what are we talking about in terms of where the abductions took place?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They took place in many areas of Kosovo but most of the largest number of abductions or in terms of geographical location took place either in the Drenica area or in the area just below it around Malisevo and Rahovec. Which is reflected in some of the cases mentioned later on in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll get to those -- actually we'll turn to them now. Now I'd like you to turn to page 78. And before we go to specifics there, could you tell us what were the findings of Human Rights Watch with regard to abductions of ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We found that -- we estimated that between 100 and 140 Serbs had been abducted by the KLA. But we recognised that the precise number was difficult to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what were your sources for information about these abductions? These particular abductions.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. They were based on information provided to us by the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had documented 138 ethnic Serbs who they believed were in KLA custody, as well as a detailed report by the Humanitarian Law Centre documented abduction of 103 ethnic Serbs for the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And were there -- were there other sources I think you might have mentioned what they were. Can you specify within the government what they were.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. On page 79 of the report, that's K0364869, we also mention some reports we had received from the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs also in August 1998, relating to their estimate that 178 individuals had been abducted in Kosovo. That includes ethnic Serbs as well as people from other nationalities as well as figures provided by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs saying that 233 civilians had been abducted by the KLA, again including people of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you've mentioned four sources: The ICRC, the Humanitarian law centre, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. How did Human Rights Watch assess the reliability of those sources?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, we are familiar with the work of the ICRC and we are working closely with the Humanitarian Law Centre. So we assessed those two sources to be of high credibility. I should point out that the report of the Humanitarian Law Centre also dealt with abductions and arbitrary arrest of ethnic Albanians, it was not just by the Yugoslav authorities. So it was not just a one-sided report on abductions by the KLA. We had greater difficulty with the reliability of the information provided to us by the Yugoslav and Serbian authorities simply because they didn't provide a lot of detail about those sources and our attempts to get greater information out of them relating to those sources were not effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: A little lower on this page that we're currently on, we have heading "Abductions in Rahovec." Could you tell us please, what were the findings there? What's that all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again. Of course it's for my learned friend to decide how he does this. It may assist -- I don't think of any of us are going to be objecting to any of these reports being admitted into evidence. The witness of course has said that they were carefully prepared and of course the reports really speak for themselves. Now of course, my learned friend may wish to elaborate or go to specific parts of it but it may not take matters much further to ask what the report says when it's before you and no doubt in due course will admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, very grateful to the counsel for any -- any assistance in helping us moving along. So I will move on to some specific instances here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can go quite quickly and quite directly to the bits that really interest you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'd like to direct your attention to page 80 which bears the ERN K0364870, the case of Jovan Lukic. Now we have the report in front of us and you will have heard what counsel has said. They -- I will direct your attention to a couple of things here. Very briefly what was this case about, Jovan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Lukic was one of the persons who was apparently detained by the KLA during their offensive on Orahovac. Many people were detained -- ethnic Serbs were detained at that time, which is what the previous section deals with. He gave a detailed statement to the Humanitarian Law Centre, which was the organisation we were working closely with, describing his detention by the KLA and some of the things he had seen while in the custody of the KLA. And he mentioned that he had been detained with many other people at a KLA-run detention facility in Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just a question about the time period and perhaps about sources as well. In that first paragraph the second sentence, sentence beginning "Tanjug reported." The sentence reads, "Tanjug reported that Lukic detained on July 19 along with Veselin Lazdjic. But the Centre mentions only Lukic being detained on July 17th." What is Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Tanjug is a Serbian news agency, which at the time was quite close to the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the Centre, the Centre there in that sentence. What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The Humanitarian Law Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now you say Tanjug was quite close to the Yugoslav authorities. In light of what you have testify today thus far, how did Human Rights Watch assess the credibility of Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We used it as a source of information but as far as possible we would always try to find corroborative evidence or [sic] any information reported there. We did view many of their reports with some suspicion. I think the bias of their reporting is shown in the title of the newspaper article we're discussing, which said "Terrorists abduct two Serbs." So they used the kind of language that we saw coming out of the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn -- thank you, Mr. Younis. We had that source and footnote now. Turning to page 81, K 0364871, the case of Vojko and Ivan Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We'll just be skipping through to a few of these cases now. What is that case about?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: T his relates to two ethnic Serbs who were taken off a bus by armed ethnic Albanians on June 29th and who were later released, according to some of the sources of information we had. Two other ethnic Serbs who were abducted together with them whose identities we didn't know remained unaccounted for. This was quite a unique case because these were ethnic Serbs, refugees from Croatia who were on their way to leaving Kosovo because they were going to be resettled by UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And your sources for that, please?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This was one of the best documented cased we had. We were able to confirm the case from UNHCR, directly. It was also included in the report, the previously mentioned report by the Humanitarian Law Centre. And it was also referred to by KLA spokesperson Jakup Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning now to page 83, K0364873. And the heading "Slobodan, Milica, and Nebojsa Radosevic." What was that case about?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This case involves three elderly Serbs who stayed behind in a village after most of the ethnic Serb population fled when the UCK took control in April 1998. It was quite typical pattern for elderly Serbs to remain behind in some of these villages just because they had nowhere to go. And the bodies of two of the people who were later found in the lake as part of a group of 34 bodies recovered by the Yugoslav authorities in Lake Radonjic near Glodjane which is on the main road from Pristina to Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the sources for that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This case was documented both by Amnesty International and it was included in the report by the Humanitarian Law Centre. And the identification of those two bodies was also reported by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did Human Rights Watch by any chance attempt to investigate this?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We were in Kosovo in early September when the Yugoslav authorities announced they found the 34 bodies in Lake Radonjic and that the bodies were being stored in a hotel in Glodjane. We travelled to Glodjane the next day to try to seek access to those bodies to look at the conditions of the bodies and attempted to determine how they were killed. And we also asked for further information from the Yugoslav authorities on these cases. By the time we reached the hotel where the bodies were being stored, they had already been moved to a morgue in Pristina and we received no cooperation from the Yugoslav authorities. However, this case was included in the six cases which were investigated by an international forensic team from Helsinki which gained access to Kosovo in November 1998, headed by Helena Romanach.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And skipping now to page 84, K0364874. The heading "Abductions of Ethnic Albanians." If you can, could you tell us first what numbers we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We were unable to establish a clear number. Clearly the number of ethnic Albanians cases -- abduction cases that had been documented at that stage were significant lower than those involving ethnic Serbs. But we had received information we considered reliable of at least some abductions of ethnic Albanians, most of them considered collaborators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what did you understand that by that phrase or that word "collaborators"?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They were either people working in some way with the Yugoslav authorities, either with the police or the security services, but also more broader: people who were suspected of working as informants or just talking a bit too much to Yugoslav or Serbian officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we can look at this mostly on our own, but I will skip now further to page 85. Heading --

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Some of the bodies which were recovered in the same incident at Lake Radonjic were the bodies of ethnic Albanians. I should mention, among the 34 bodies which were found were the bodies of some ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And would it be right that in that case Human Rights Watch would have had the same difficulties --

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- investigating that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The next page, page 85. K0364875, heading "Restrictions on the Media." I believe there are two cases set out here. Could you tell us about the first one.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. The first one occurred in August 1998. It involved two ethnic Serbian -- well, an ethnic Serbian journalist and his driver working for the pro-Yugoslav government, Radio Pristina. They were -- they went missing near city of Orahovac and it was feared that they were abducted by the KLA. We spoke to officials at Radio Pristina to get the basic information, which was not very clear because they will left and disappeared on the road and had basically gone missing. The KLA never acknowledged having those two people in their detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one moment please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher if I could show you a document, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Or actually you could probably just turn to it yourself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Quickly, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This is a document that we issued after talking to sources at Radio Pristina as well as other people in Kosovo expressing our concern abduction of the journalist and the driver and asking for their immediate release and setting out the circumstances that we were able to find about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This was a press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Why does Human Rights Watch issue a document like this?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Because we wanted to immediately respond to the abduction of these two journalists and try to seek their release. All of these press releases were translated into Albanian and published in local newspapers like Koha Ditore. So it was a direct communication channel to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So when you say "all of the press releases," you're saying that this particular document was also translated into Albanian?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It wasn't translated into Albanian by us, it was translated into Albanian by Koha Ditore and certain other newspapers. But Koha Ditore had a policy of ensuring that all of our statements both about Yugoslav and KLA abuses were translated and published in their newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Prior to this document being issued and as it's dated 26th of August, and I believe that's 1998?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Does Human Rights Watch -- did they publish -- issue, sorry issue other press releases in connection with work in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the same statement, on the right side of the page under "Related Material" are some other press releases that we issued in the few months before then, just to give you a few examples. The first one dealt with a the ethnic Albanian journalist being arrested in Kosovo; the second dealt with A protest about academic freedom in Serbia; the third dealt with ethnic Albanian human rights lawyer arrested by Yugoslav authorities and being abused. And obviously there is many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the most effective way of handling this might be. If this could be given a number, or perhaps it would be better to give the bundle of documents a number and remain with the tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps each document, from the Defence point of view, should be given a separate exhibit number. I say that because tab 3 is not complete and my learned friend has said that he will provide you with a complete version of that report and upon that basis tab 3 will not be objected to; but perhaps each document can be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you got any comment on tab 3, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No. I did discuss this with counsel beforehand. I was perhaps under the mistaken understanding that some parts of these documents will be objected to. I understand that is not the case now. We have perfectly happy to have the entirety of tab 3 submitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And is that available?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My understanding is it is available. So perhaps we could just interpose that and just have it given one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What i would propose is to delay the reception of this until tab 3 completed and then admit the whole document as one exhibit, the whole bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Your Honour. In that case I will proceed with the documents and at the enter seek a number for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, directing your attention now back to page 85 of "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo," that's K0364875. You've told us about one case. What's -- could you tell us about the second case there.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. In the second case, two journalists working for Tanjug, a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. journalist and a photographer, were arrested by the KLA. And we issued a similar statement, press release about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And who were these journalists?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Their name were Nebojsa Radosevic and Vladimir Dobricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where were they abducted?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They were abducted near the village of Magure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We'll talk about more about this incident later. If you could just tell us what your sources were for the material on this case in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I do object. You have the report before you. The witness used the word "arrested." My friend has used the word "abducted." The report say "captured." Your Honours, I would ask that evidence not be put in the witness' mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I may respond. The report itself does use the word "abductions." I do accept that the witness said "arrested" and I'm happy to use that word, if appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This incident, if you could just tell us your source, please, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well this was quite a solidly confirmed case. Initially, when these -- this case came to your attention the two journalists had just gone missing. But a few days afterwards we were able to confirm through the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, that these two people were in KLA custody. And later the KLA issued a statement saying that the two people had been sentenced to 60 days in prison number 7, for -- convicted on spying charges. So we were able to confirm this case by several sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention to tab number 7. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This was the statement that we issued after we were able to confirm the -- can I say arrest? Of these two journalists with the ICRC. And the like the earlier statement, it calls for their release.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was this -- this is a press release; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And was this also translated into Albanian?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And who did that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm certain it was -- it was published in the Koha Ditore newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And turning to page 86, K 036 -- sorry. I think I had my microphone off. Turning to page 86, K 0364876. And as we get that on Sanction. Sorry 4876. I'm very grateful to Mr. Younis for his assistance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The paragraph in the middle of the page beginning on: "On October 14th." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: On August 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry on August 14th.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this incident was about?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It involved close friend of us, Stacey Sullivan, who was a journalist working mostly for the New York Times. She was stopped by a group of KLA soldiers while interviewing ethnic Albanian civilians and the soldiers grabbed her notebook and burned some pages out of her notebook. She had gone -- she then went to complain to a regional commander and the commander apologised to her and said that the soldiers will be stripped of -- that he had stripped the soldiers of his weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be preferable if we ran for another ten minutes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention now to page 11 of the report which has the ERN number K0364801. And if you just give us a minute while we bring that up on Sanction. That's fine, thank you. And I'm going to direct your attention to the heading "To the UCK" -- I won't try that pronunciation. Can you tell us first of all what is in this section? Could you describe to us what it is.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This section comes immediately after the executive summary of the report and makes recommendations to the various parties -- to the conflict in Kosovo as well as to the international community on how to end the abuses in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And now I'll direct your attention now to the first bullet point there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't have microphone on. I will repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll direct your attention to the first bullet point there. The last sentence there reads, "In particular the UCK should release all civilians in detention." Now this is a recommendation to the KLA. Apart from publication in here, was there any other way in which it was conveyed to them?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Our first meeting with the KLA took place in November 1998 when we discussed many of these issues. But in general, as I said before, the ethnic Albanian newspapers in Kosovo, particularly the Koha Ditore newspaper, made it a policy to quote extensively from our reports in some cases even serially reproduced entire reports in the newspaper and we also provided a copy of this report to the political representative of the KLA, Adem Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What language was that done in?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's press reports would have been in the Albanian language. We also gave extensive interviews about this report in two ethnic Albanian newspapers, which addressed specifically both the Yugoslav army abuses as well as the KLA abuses. The report that was handed over to Adem Demaqi would have been in English because he is a fluent English speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned in one of the cases we discussed earlier that a source was Jakup Krasniqi. Could you explain that now, please?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Jakup Krasniqi was one of the main spokespersons for the Kosovo Liberation Army and he gave an extensive interview to Koha Ditore in which he mentioned the cases of these two -- these two ethnic Serbs from Croatia who had been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And is this included in the report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes it's included in the report. I would have to find it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps it will save time if I -- thank you to counsel. If I just direct you to page 76. Sorry. The ERN is K0364866?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Two paragraphs at the top of the page, starting with "the UCK has never dealt with civilians" are an excerpt from the interview of Jakup Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we see in the second paragraph, just to move things along, we see a reference to the handing over of two Serbs.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes He said, "A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross. Those we have kidnapped are either announced in a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And do you have other sources from the KLA set out here?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. At the bottom of the page is a statement made by Shaban Shala, who is a KLA commander, formerly a human rights activist for the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And turning to page 77 which is K0364867. This is a continuation of what appears to be an excerpt from this interview with Shaban Shala. I'll direct your attention to that last sentence, since we can read the rest ourselves: "There are cases when individuals make mistakes but such cases are punished by the UCK even if the soldiers conducted them." Can you comment on that the last sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We were very keen to get more information about the UCK and its internal code of conduct and disciplinary procedures as well as evidence that they had actually punished some of their members for violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You had mentioned Adem Demaqi. The next paragraph on that page refers to, or makes refers to Adem Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could just have that brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And there's a brief quote from him which we can read. But I'll just direct your attention. Let me just read it; perhaps it will be faster. "When I talked to certain people form the headquarters I saw that there was a united view on one thing. We did not deal in kidnappings" -- I'm cautioned to go slow -- "and some groups do it on their own. And if we have influential on them, we always intervene and kidnapped persons are released." Now, that reference from the headquarters, do you know what that is in reference to?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We understood it to be a reference to the general headquarters of the KLA which was a body which was mentioned in quite a few of the statements issued by the KLA. They would issue official statements which were handed over to us through various sources referring to their general headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes it for that document so this may be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. We will have the first adjournment now. There are circumstances which require us to have a half-hour break at this time rather than the 20 minutes. So we will resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Younis informs me that we have now distributed tab number 3 in its entirety. So perhaps this would be a good point to receive a number. The only point I would raise is that tabs -- there are nine tabs in all, firstly; secondly, tabs 1 and 2 are previously -- previously tendered exhibits. So this exhibit, if I could suggest, might perhaps be given a number with only tabs 3 through 9. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tabs 1 and 3 are already exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In fact tab 1 and 2 are previous exhibits in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Separately tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 1 is actually P048 and tab 2 is P138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do an imprecise thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tab 3 onwards of this bundle will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tabs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 will be Prosecution Exhibit P212.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And apologise Your Honours for bringing about this imprecision in our system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that is the worst that happen procedurally, we will be in good order, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Hopefully that will only be it's worst that happens. A final point is that tab 9 is also only excerpts from a document but I have not heard from counsel as to whether they have any problems with that. The bulk of that document in fact deals primarily with events in 1999. And I -- it's a rather large document which is why I had excerpted only directly relevant sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Well, we have received tabs 3 to 9 as Exhibit P212, tabs and 2 being previously exhibits. And in the absence of any other sign, you can move on, Mr. Shin. And the indications are very clear that you can go as directly and as quickly as you can be encouraged to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. As I explained to counsel during the break I had indeed been under a mistaken but perhaps not so mistaken impression that there may have been more difficulty. But I am grateful that we are in agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'd like to show you a document. In fact you can just turn to it yourself. That's tab number 4.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This -- could you just tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's a Human Rights Watch report researched by Fred Abrahams and myself during our September 1998 mission to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the title of that report is "Detentions and abuses in Kosovo"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's also given a heading "Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When was this report issued?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was issued in December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could briefly, what detention and abuse there Kosovo is this report about?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It deals with abuses, detention abuses committed by both the Yugoslav forces and Kosovo Liberation Army. It documents a significant number of deaths in custody as well as detention abuses committed by Yugoslav and Serbian authorities as well as the very negative role plaided by the Serbian judiciary in these abuses. And it has a short chapter summarizing some of our findings in terms of detention and abuse by KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where can we find that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It starts on page 23 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And page 23 is ERN 00676492?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I have been turning the microphone off out of habit. I will stop doing that. Page 23 is 00676492. And how far does this section go?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It goes to page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Which is the same ERN number, ending 94. Mr. Bouckaert, you explained to us that this report derives from work that you and Mr. Abrahams did in September of 1998 in Kosovo. What time period is covered by the detentions and abuse by the KLA that are addressed in this report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: As the section on the KLA says, it deals with abuses committed since February 1998 up to the publication of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And where did these detentions and abuse -- where did they take place?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They took place in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If possible, could you tell us more specifically where in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well it took place in many areas of Kosovo and as we had previously discussed, we concluded that between at least 100 and possibly as many as 300 people had been abducted by the KLA and there are some details from some of those cases included in this short section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
