utterances.text: And we ask see that in the report itself. If I can direct your attention to a couple of particular sections in the third paragraph beginning: "The ICRC." The report reads, I quote: The ICRC has been denied access to KLA detainees, which raises suspicions about their safety." And it goes to on to refer to a quote an ICRC representative. Could you comment, please, on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It's very usual for the ICRC to speak so publicly about access problems as well as abuse problems, which I think is an indication of how seriously the ICRC was concerned about their lack of access to facilities as well as about the general pattern of abuses they were documenting. We obviously had our own discussions with the ICRC which we consider confidential, which discussed the same concerns and abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph reads: "On a number of occasions, the KLA has released people in its custody. On July 22nd, the KLA handed 35 ethnic Serb civilians over to the ICRC after they had been detained on July 19th during fighting in Orahovac." Could you please comment on that.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. That -- those ethnic Serbs who were handed over to the ICRC were part of a larger group of ethnic Serbs who were -- who went missing during the KLA's brief seizure of Orahovac, some of whom were still missing at the time of the publication of our report. There is also the case of the two ethnic Serbs from Croatia who were handed over to the ICRC, which we discussed in the earlier session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this section that we've just looked at beginning on a number of occasions, there's no footnote to that. Can you please tell us your sources for that.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Actually, there is a public source for that. The same information is included in the humanitarian law violations report. In Kosovo report citing an ICRC statement which was issued at the time, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The paragraph on the bottom, beginning "On October 18th." Could you tell us what case is addressed there.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This is the case of the two Serbian journalists which we discussed during the earlier session, the two Serbian journalists who went missing and were later acknowledged to be in KLA detention on October 18.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We will turn to that in some detail shortly. On the next page, page 25, the first full paragraph beginning, on November 27th. If you could read that and tell us what that is about.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'll read the paragraph. It says: "On November 27 in honour of Albanian flag day, the KLA released the two journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Please go slowly.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: In the presence of U.S. diplomat William Walker who heads the Organization for Security and Cooperation (OSCE) mission in Kosovo. "Two ethnic Albanian political activists from the Democratic League of Kosovo in Malisevo, Jakup Kastrati and Cen Desku, who had been in KLA detention for three weeks, were also amnestied. A KLA communique released on November 27" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, if you could please read and pause between phrases and sentences.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: "A KLA communique released on November 27 said the amnesty demonstrated the KLA's commitment to international conventions governing warfare. On November 24th, the KLA released a Serb policeman after U.S. diplomatic intervention."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us about these two ethnic Albanian political activists who had been amnestied. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They were LDK activists from Malisevo. I don't have any other details about them, other than they had been in KLA custody for a period Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of about three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What is your source for the information that they had been held in KLA detention for three weeks and were also amnestied?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The KLA issued a public statement which is referred to in this paragraph, relating to go these releases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that next paragraph beginning: "Two other journalists." I believe that is a case that have you told about already; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the two journalists who had been earlier arrested in August -- or who had gone missing, I should say, in August. The KLA never acknowledged their detention and they remained missing at the time of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the previous report we had seen a section with recommendations to the KLA. Does this report have any recommendations to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I believe it does. They are found on page 6 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That is ERN 00676465.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was this report provided to anyone in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: In between the publication of the first report we discussed and this report, we had a meet with the KLA at which we discussed our concerns and raised our recommendation as well. And as usual, we provided this report, as all of other reports and information, to the ethnic Albanian press as well as to the office of Adem Demaqi which was also the communication channel which was suggested to us by the KLA representatives who we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were any press releases issued in connection with this report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. All of our reports are accompanied by a press release which summarises our report and alerts the press to the existence of the report. And also gives them some quotes from -- normally from the head of the division to use in their newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention now to tab 3. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: You've cut off my picture a little bit, but it's a report that I wrote, called "A Week of Terror in Drenica: Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was there a picture on the cover?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah. It seems like a white page kind of cutting off the top half of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's not hiding anything significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. When was this report issued?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This report was issued in February 1998 -- 1999, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was your involvement in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I was the primary researcher as well as the author of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could tell us briefly what is this report about.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It deals with a week in September 1998 in which some of the most severe violations by Yugoslav forces were committed up to that stage in the conflict. We had been present in Kosovo at this time, and had personally witnessed and visited the sites of these massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention with regards to this report simply to two pages. That would be pages 8 and 9. That would be the ERN pages K0364938 and K0364939. Again, these are recommendations to the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were these also translated, these recommendations?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I believe at this time our summary and the recommendations of the reports were translated at least into Serbian and possibly also into Albanian by Human Rights Watch. But they certainly also would have been picked up by the locally Albanian press. And as with all of our reports they were handed over to Adem Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we can read these for ourselves. But just to direct your attention to two points. The first bullet point on page 8, K0364938. It begins: "Release all civilians in detention." It continues on after that. This report is about, as you have explained to us abuses committed by Serbian forces. Why would this recommendation appear in that report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, because we continue to have the same concerns about abductions and the fate of ethnic Serbs and ethnic Albanians abducted by the KLA. I must say, we also had a much more positive reception for our recommendations from the KLA. So we felt it was important to continue that dialogue with the KLA about their own conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And turning to the next page, K0364939, page 9 of the report itself. At the top the first bullet point there: "Bring to justice commanders and troops guilty of these violations in conformity of international standards of due process." Could you comment on the that, please?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We felt important for the KLA to uphold international humanitarian law, but also to implement international humanitarian law by punishing its troops and its commanders when abused were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, turning away from these reports for the time being. You have referred to the conflict a number of times. Could you tell us who were the parties to the conflict. The Judges will have heard a lot of evidence on this, so you can be brief just to indicate who you mean.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The parties involved both Yugoslav and Serbian forces on one side, as well as some irregular paramilitary formation on the side of the government. And then the Kosovo Liberation Army as well as other armed Albanian elements on the other side of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, just taking the Yugoslav and Serbian forces first. Did Human Rights Watch research or investigate anything about those forces?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I think we listed some of the command structure of these forces in the "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo" report, starting with Slobodan Milosevic down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And again with regards to these Yugoslav and Serbian forces, you've mentioned now the command structure. Was there anything else that was researched or investigated?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, again, I think it's important to remember that we were working in a very difficult environment with an active conflict going on. And certainly our later reports such as the other orders report which we issued after the end of the conflict in Kosovo were much more detailed about the information that we were able to assemble about the command structure of the Yugoslavia army as well as the forces involved in the fighting in Kosovo. At this early stage, we could have at least determine that the fighting involved the Yugoslav army itself, as well as the MUP forces under the command of the Ministry of Interior. And we also had pretty convincing reports that some other organisations such as the special anti-terrorist police under the command of Frankie -- I forget his last name, but known as Frankie's boys were involved in some of the fighting. As well as some armed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What time period are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time period February to the publication these reports, February 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning to the other side of the conflict, KLA. Did Human Rights Watch likewise investigate or research anything about -- about them?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, our "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo" report as well as later reports includes extensive analysis of the applicability of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions as well as Protocol 1 Additional to the Geneva Conventions. So for that analysis, we did have to look extensively at the nature of the KLA and its organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just staying with the KLA now. What factors did you look to in your analysis, the analysis that you just described?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We looked at the level of organisation of their forces; issues such as whether they were in uniform, whether there seemed to be a general command structure of the sources of their funding. What else? The existence of a high command. Issues such as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just taking these one at a time. What were Human Rights Watch's findings with regard to the level of organisation of their forces?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, the level of organisation of the KLA evolved over time. They had been quite active even before February 1998, especially in the Drenica area of Kosovo. By the period that we are talking about now, February 1998, they certainly seemed to have become more organised. Most of their soldiers were in uniform with UCK badges identifying their allegiance. And it seemed like there were a number of zonal commanders which according to the sources that we had available to us, were represented on a high command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you mentioned that was in the humanitarian law violations report, these findings. Before we turn to that could you tell us how did Human Rights Watch come to these findings?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, they're based on own observations out in the field. Here I would have to restrict my testimony to my missions in September and November 1998. But certainly, my colleague Fred Abrahams also had own authorisations based on his earlier missions as well as our extensive contacts with journalists, especially journalists from newspapers like Koha Ditore which regularly interviewed KLA commanders and were quite familiar with the names of commanders and the structure of the organisation; as well as the ICRC, the Kosovo diplomatic observer commission, international journalists, and locally human rights groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where in "humanitarian law violations" we would be able to find these issues addressed. Tab 5?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah. It would be in chapter 11 of the report which is called "Legal Standards and the Kosovo Conflict," which starts on page 88. The discussion relating to the KLA starts on page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's ERN K0364882 for page 92; and the section began on page 88 of the report, which is the the ERN number K0364878.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 92. I would just like to you ask you to explain in further detail. Again we had the page before us if you could just explain to us some of the information set out on this page. The first sentence reads: "Although the UCK is primarily a guerrilla army with no rigid hierarchical structure and there are separate internal factions, during the period covered by this report (from February to September), the UCK was an organised military force for the purposes of international humanitarian law." This phrase, "no rigid hierarchical structure," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It means that their command structure at that stage was relatively fluid and did not always include formal ranks of officers. And it was often difficult for us to -- in the field to understand where different commander fit into the structure of the UCK. So it would be more accurate as we talk, as we describe a few sentences later to talk about regional and subregional commander with people under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just your answer there so we're clear, what time period are we talking about? Is it February to September as set out in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, correct. But over that period command structure did become nor formalised. So we are talking about a situation of significant fluidity. But it certainly -- that description would go back all the way to February 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could just skip to the last sentence that that paragraph, which -- sorry, second-to-last sentence. Which reads: "Not all but most of the regional commanders were represented in the high command, the body within the UCK that makes decision for the whole UCK." What time period are we talking about it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It will be for that same time period. Although the use of the term "high command," it would probably have been more accurate to use the term "general headquarters," which was the term used by the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: A few more questions on this page. In the next paragraph, first sentence. There's a reference to checkpoints and policies and procedures. Could you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. One of the biggest frustrations that journalists and observers had in Kosovo is that we would be very frequently stopped at checkpoints and asked for travel permission from the KLA. And that travel permission had to come from Adem Demaqi. And if we couldn't produce the permission we would frequently be told to turn back. But unfortunately, Adem Demaqi only issued travel permission for one day and didn't get up early in the morning on some days. So it created a lot of frustration and difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if you could just remind us again who is Adem Demaqi? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: He was the Pristina-based political representative of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we look a little further down in that same paragraph, it's the third sentence from the bottom beginning with the word "despite"?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That sentence reads -- "Despite this." I believe that's a reference to a lack of discipline. "It is clear that the UCK leadership was able to organise systematic attacks throughout large parts of Kosovo." What large parts of Kosovo are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, it would include the quite significant offensive that the UCK undertook after the February/March atrocities committed by the Yugoslav forces that we discussed earlier which led to them seizing control of most of Drenica, the central region of Kosovo, which is mostly a rural area, as well as the offensive -- the relatively unsuccessful offensive on the city of Orahovac which was the only time that the UCK tried to take a big city and it did seize control for that big city for a period of two days. So those offensive actions would have involved the coordination of quite a significant number of fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just one more question on this page. The next paragraph. Sorry, Mr. Bouckaert, you wanted to say something else?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah. I think a very relevant factor is also the sentence preceding what we just discussed or sorry, after what we just discussed which is the financial -- the coordination of the financial support into Kosovo and weapons into Kosovo which were distributed throughout the province by the KLA and which again indicated to us quite a significant ability to coordinate on the part of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph beginning: "From April until mid-July 1998, the UCK held as much as 40 per cent of the territory of Kosovo, although most of that territory was retain by government forces by August 1998." Could you please explain how Human Rights Watch came about that figure of 40 per cent?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. The area controlled by UCK at that stage involved most of Drenica as well as the area below Drenica around Malisevo and town such as that. So basically we just looked at a map and consulted with other organisations, including the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission and concluded that was the about the percentage of territory. Most of it rural territory which the UCK controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We have the rest of this section to review your findings, so I won't go into detail any further on that. Let me turn to another area. You have made reference previously to the intensification of the armed conflict of February 1998. Could you tell us briefly, what happened in February 1998? What do you mean by the intensification?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: As documented in the report and was researched by my fellow researcher, Fred Abrahams, a watershed event in the Kosovo conflict was a series of attacks by the Yugoslav forces on three villages in Drenica, which led to very grave massacres, was the village of Kirez [phoen], Donji Prekaz, and I think Likoshan. Apparently, in terms of the watershed nature of the event, especially the killing of almost the entire family of Adem Jashari who was a main -- was seen as a main KLA leader really changed the situation on the ground. Some of the funerals of the victims of the these massacres were attended by tens of thousands of people, and allowed the KLA to recruit a large number of people and to massively expand its operations. It really changed the situation on the ground in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And perhaps following on that, how would you characterise -- when you say intensification, how would you characterise the level of the conflict after what you have just described?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Starting in February 1998 when we started to see the use of really typical military-style equipment and tactics by the Yugoslav forces including helicopters and tanks and armoured vehicles, and since late February 1998 there was almost constant fighting with brief pauses in the fighting, shifting from these massacres that I just described and to the border between Kosovo and Albania and then back to the central areas of Kosovo as the KLA went on the offensive and took control of significant parts of Kosovo and then towards the end of the summer, a massive Yugoslav offensive started to retake those areas which resulted in some of the massacres described in my report, "A Week of Terror in Drenica." That is a very brief summary of the events which are described in the "Humanitarian Law in Kosovo" report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this conflict, when did the conflict end?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The conflict didn't really end. There were brief pauses after Holbrooke and Milosevic came to an agreement with the first threat of NATO bombing of Kosovo. Milosevic promised to withdraw most of the troops from Kosovo. He didn't comply with that agreement. There was the Racak massacre, which is also described in our reports. And ultimately it led to the NATO intervention in Kosovo. So the conflict only ended with the withdrawal of Yugoslav forces after the end of the NATO war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've made reference to organisational structures. Did Human Rights Watch investigate disciplinary issues on both sides?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what were its findings with regards to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Let me first say that with regards to the Yugoslav forces their forces acted with complete impunity on the ground. The situation was a little bit more complex with the KLA. They claimed to us that they had disciplinary procedures in place, but through our entire period of research, aside from the relatively minor incident involving Stacey Sullivan the journalist who had notebook burned, we didn't document a single case in which the KLA disciplined or punished their own troops despite our repeated requested from them to provide that information. To them, I should say, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, Mr. Bouckaert, to, or rather return to the issue of the missing Tanjug journalists. You had told us that one KLA source for this -- for Human Rights Watch's findings was Jakup Krasniqi, his interview. Did you have another KLA source for that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: For which particular case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: For the missing journalists, missing journalists?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Krasniqi was a source for the two Serbian, Croatia people who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. went missing. In terms of the two Serbian journalists there was the ICRC and Adem Demaqi, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what did Human Rights Watch do in terms of follow-up for this case?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We asked through an intermediary to meet with members of the KLA general headquarters to discuss this case as well as other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did the intermediary arrange a meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The meeting took place on November 10, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what was your purpose in arranged this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We wanted to establish a channel of communications with the KLA, explain our work in Kosovo, inform them of their international obligations under the laws of war and raise the concern of these specific two journalists as well as asking them some questions about their code of conduct and other issues of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Where was meeting held?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We were asked to go to the town of Malisevo and we waited there until we were met by two KLA representatives. And they then took us to the meeting place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was myself, Fred Abrahams and the local intermediary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you went to this town, and I believe you said it was a town near Malisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They arrived in a white Niva jeep in military uniform and asked us to accompany them. They drove to us a farmhouse in a town called Banja. We entered the farmhouse. It was just a regular house, not any kind of military structure. And then sat down in a room for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you there to ask you: When they drove you, I gather you were in their car.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. We were in our own car. We followed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What -- did these two persons, did they introduce themselves when you met them before following them?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We, we immediately recognised one of them as Hashim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the other, at that point, did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How did the meeting begin?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We went around and introduced our ourselves. First they introduced themselves and then we introduced ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How many persons were in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was ourselves, the three people, me, Fred Abrahams and our intermediary, as well as the two KLA representatives. There was elderly man in the house but he didn't participate in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And by the way, what time of day was this?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We met them -- we drove down from Pristina around 9.00 and probably met them around 10.30 a.m. So meeting started about 11.00 a.m. and lasted for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How did the two KLA representatives introduce themselves? If you could take one at a time.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi introduced himself first. Said he was in charge of the -- head of the political department of the general headquarters of the KLA. Then the second person introduced themselves as Celiku and said he was head of the legal department of the general headquarters of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I gather that you and Fred Abrahams introduced yourselves as well.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Then we introduced ourselves and explained the work of Human Rights Watch in Kosovo from -- going back to our early work, beginning in 1990 as well as our work during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the response to your explanation about the work of Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The KLA representatives expressed their gratitude and appreciation for the work of Human Rights Watch and seemed familiar with our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you say "the KLA representatives," can you be more precise as to who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's impossible for me to say who exactly said what. In general, I would say that Mr. Thaqi seemed senior in rank to Mr. Celiku. He did most of the talking during the meeting, but Mr. Celiku also actively participated during the entire meeting. I think at this stage it was Mr. Thaqi who expressed his appreciation for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the next issue that you discuss?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: After generally describing our work and being thanked by Mr. Thaqi the KLA representatives, we said we were also investigating abuses by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the response to that, if any?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, as soon as we said that, Mr. Thaqi interrupted us and said, Yes, we know that abuses do occur during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Then what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We went into some greater depth about the kind of concerns that we had about the KLA. The -- there was a discussion which went back and forth between two issues, one of them being the KLA's code of conduct and the second being the two journalists who had been detained by the KLA in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could take those issues one at a time. The code of conduct, how did the issue of the code of conduct come up?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, after Mr. Thaqi said abuses do occur in wartime, we said -- I as a lawyer gave a brief explanation of their obligations under international law and Mr. Thaqi responded saying, Yes, we have a code of conduct to address these issues. We then asked if we could see a copy of that code of conduct and they said that no, because of military secrecy or something, they would be not be able to provide us with that code of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And it may be impossible for you to recall now and if that's the case just indicate that. When they said no, do you recall who said no, you would not be able to see code of conduct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I believe it was Mr. Thaqi. But Mr. Celiku did participate in this discussion and talked a little bit about the kind of civilian structures that they were trying to create in the areas under their control, to implement -- to ensure the rule of law in the areas under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a minute. If I could just ask you first: You raised the matter of international law and Mr. Thaqi responded by discussing the code of conduct. Did Mr. Thaqi or Mr. Celiku have any other responses to the issue of international law? Is there anything else that they said?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. But they seemed generally familiar with their obligations under the Geneva Conventions and acknowledged that the KLA would abide by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, turning back to what you were just telling us about the civilian structures to implement the rule of law. That was, as you were saying, Mr. Celiku who was addressing that. Can you tell us anything more about that, what was said?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact statement that Mr. Celiku made. But he was basically trying to explain to us that the KLA was an army under pressure; that, you know, they were trying to create structures and that one of the things try to do was create civilian structures under -- in so-called liberated areas and he discussed some of the difficulties they had doing that. We returned to this topic later on when we discussed the case of these two journalists who had -- who were in KLA custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Why don't we turn to that now, the two journalists. How did the discussion on the two journalists begin?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We initiated that discussion saying that we were particularly concerned about these two journalists who had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what was the response, if any? And if there was a response, who responded?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We then had an in-depth discussion about the case of these two journalists. I recall that Mr. Thaqi presented his frustration about the attention the case of these two journalists had generated, pointing out the fact that many Albanian journalists and human rights activists had been abused by the Yugoslav forces. Then we asked some very specific questions about -- they said -- sorry. They said that these two journalists had been tried and convicted by a court. And then we asked some very specific questions about the nature of this trial. We asked if they had been represented by counsel. The response was that counsel had been invited, but had not shown up. We asked if the two persons had been present during their trial and the answer was that they had not been present. We then asked if they had been informed of the charges against them, and if they had -- had adequate time to prepare and present defence and became clear to us that was also not the case. The KLA representatives tried to indicate to us there were more serious charges than spying but did not go into detail about this. So after this discussion, I made the point to them, that we [Realtime transcript read in error: "they"] felt this trial had fallen short of international standards and that the journalists should be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And before we continue on that, just looking back over what you have just told us about the discussion about the two journalists. You say "they," they responded, speaking of the two KLA representatives. If you can, please be more clear who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I recall that both of them actively participated in this discussion and both familiar with the details of this trial. And we had specifically asked our intermediary for a meeting with the KLA to discuss this case and I believe that Mr. Celiku was part of the KLA delegation at this meeting because he was in charge of the legal department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you say that there's reference to more potentially -- charges potentially more serious than spying. Do we understand from that that spying was the charge that these persons were convicted of or was that explained or addressed?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Through our sources we already knew that the men had been convicted of spying and sentenced to 60 days in KLA prison number 7 which is a prison that we were not familiar with and we didn't know the location of that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could be a little more clear about that. Who told you about -- who told you that they were being held in prison number seven?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They were -- it was through journalists at Koha Ditore that we received this information. I'm not sure if the KLA issued a formal statement affirming this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, was there a reference to prison number 7 during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the actual location was discussed. However, we did ask for -- after -- I should continue with the chronology of the meeting. After I asked if the -- said that the trial was not in accordance with international standards and asked for the journalists to be released, we were told by -- I believe Mr. Celiku that this was a matter for the judicial authorities and they didn't want to interfere with the independence of their judicial authorities and that the case would go on appeal. So at that stage we asked for -- they also told us that it's prisoners were in good health and not been abused. So we asked for access to the prisoners as well as access to the appeal hearing. Unfortunately, like our earlier request, that request was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And again, just so we are clear who was doing the talking when you were talking about this case?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I believe on the point of judicial independence it was Celiku who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: For the record, I wonder if my friend could perhaps press and try and get an answer from the witness regarding the question as to whether or not it's being said now, today, that something about prison number 7 was mentioned in that meeting. There was no answer that I could see to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall if prison number 7 was mentioned in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you talked about this request to have access to the prisoners as well the appeal hearing and you say the requests were denied. Were they denied during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if you can, do you recall who it was who denied those requests?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was there a reason given as to why you could not visit the prisoners where they were being held?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I believe the general reason why most of our requests were denied was because of military secrecy. They did say that if we wanted to make appeal to the appeals court, that we could do so through the office of Adem Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You say, you believe was military secrecy. Let me put it this way. What is your basis for believing that the reason was military secrecy?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I clearly recall that they denied our request to see their code of conduct on the basis of military secrecy. I don't recall their exact reasoning of we could not visit the prison. So perhaps it will be better for me to say that I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just -- I believe you told us that you were told in this meeting that the condition of these detainees was that they were fine?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you can, can you recall who it was that told you that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. That was Mr. Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you don't speak Albanian, from what you told us earlier. How was the meeting conducted in terms of the language?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The intermediary also served as our interpreter. And Fred Abrahams, my colleague, does speak Albanian. But it was translated for my benefit, the entire meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When told that you would not have access to the appeal, did the discussion move on to any other topics?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We did discuss a few other topics. After this we also suggested an alternative way for these persons to be released if there really wasn't an issue of judicial independence involved, would be for general headquarters to amnesty the prisoners and we offered to help facilitate the amnesty and the release of the two detainees. And we argued strongly for the public relations benefits that this will have to the KLA, to amnesty these persons. We did briefly return -- then we also discussed -- do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We discussed also cooperation by the KLA with ourselves and also the Office of the Prosecutor of the Yugoslav Tribunal on the issues of war crimes, particularly in terms of identification of Yugoslav officials involved in war crimes. And then a final topic which was discussed is whether or not the KLA had taken any disciplinary proceedings against individual members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what were you told by the KLA representatives on that last topic?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We were told by Mr. Thaqi that there had been disciplinary proceedings against some KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did he provide any details?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We specifically asked him details and said that if he could provide us with details, or if they could provide us with details, that we would include those details in our own reports to show that KLA was not just talking about its commitment to the Geneva Conventions but also actively implementing it, but did not provide us with any cases, any details of any cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you provided with any details of any cases after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. As we make clear in post-conflict report, under orders ^ name of report?, we never received any information from the KLA about specific instances in which they disciplined or punished their soldiers for abuses committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now you told us that Mr. Celiku had introduced himself as, I believe you said the legal department?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: He said that he was the head of the legal department of the general headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did he explain what that meant?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: On the day of that meeting, did you know Mr. Celiku by any other name?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. I didn't know him by the name of Celiku either prior to the meeting. We had never met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you later learn of -- did you later learn that he a name other than Celiku?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague Fred Abrahams established quite quickly after the meeting that his name was Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How long did this meeting take place.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It lasts for about two hours. And it ended on a very amicable note. We were very pleased that the KLA had entered into such a serious discussion with us and still remained very pleased by the fact that the KLA was willing to engage with us on these issues, unlike the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The events -- this meeting itself and the contents of this meeting, were they reported in any of the reports of Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps to save time I will just direct you first to a -- detentions and abuses, that report.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. They are included in a paragraph on page -- the last paragraph on page 24, going into page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's tab 4, Your Honours. And Page 24 -- pages 24 and 25 would be ERN 00676493, 00676494?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was there also another report within which you reported this meeting and the contents of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. There was an internal note about this meeting but there was also a mention of this meeting in our -- under "orders report," which is -- I think is included as tab 9. I hope it was copied. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just to save time, I will direct you to page 492 and you can tell me if what is the correct reference.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It's also mentioned someplace else in the report but this is one of the two places, in the last paragraph it's 492, going into 493.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours that's page 492 and 493, at the last tab bearing the ERN numbers K0361326 and 1327. That's a section beginning on 1326 with the sentence: "In November 1998 Human Rights Watch researchers had a meeting with two KLA representatives. Hashim Thaqi and Fatmir Limaj to discuss KLA's commitment to the laws of war." Mr. Bouckaert, when was this report under orders published or released it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was released -- I believe it was October 2001 if I may just double-check. Yes, October 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Human Rights Watch take any other actions in connection with this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, we wrote a letter to thank of KLA for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would refer you to tab 8. That's ERN it's a one-page document ERN U0081346. Is this the letter you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could just ask you a few questions about this letter. First, who wrote this letter?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Fred Abrahams wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we have a date, 2nd December, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who was this addressed to?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: As it says on the top of the page it was addressed to the general political representative of the KLA, which is Mr. Adem Demaqi. The political directorate of the general headquarters headed by Hashim Thaqi, and the judicial directorate of the general headquarters headed by Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, how do you know that Fatmir Limaj was the head of the judicial directorate of the general headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Because that is how he identified himself as during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We can read the letter for ourselves. I'll just ask you a few questions about it in detail. I'm sorry. We'll be doing this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could actually have the letter placed on the ELMO, we'll do it the old-fashioned way, since this is not on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in that first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the first paragraph a reference to two meetings in mid-November with Mr. Adem Demaqi and Mr. Hashim Thaqi. Is the mid-November meeting with Hashim Thaqi the meeting that you've just told us about in Banja?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'm sorry Mr. Limaj's name wasn't included.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Why wasn't Mr. Limaj's name included.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Because Hashim Thaqi was seen as the big fish. He was the -- seen as the public head of the KLA, so in our haste, I guess we left off Mr. Limaj's name. I hope he is not offended?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you know the name Fatmir Limaj when this letter was prepared?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I actually didn't find out Mr. Limaj's name for quite bit of time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You have explained to us that the reference to the judicial directorate appears at the top of the letter?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Most of it's colour commanders were moan by that time as noms de guerre. They all had names like Celiku or Snake or Tiger. I remember when we left the meeting we were joking that they could start a zoo if they -- even if they lost the war because a lot of their names were animal names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning to the second paragraph. There's a reference to the recent decision to release the two Tanjug journalists as with well two Albanian political activists?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall when these releases took place?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was in late November. The exact date is in our detentions report. We addressed it a little bit earlier in my testimony. I don't want to guess, but I think it was November 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. But we can find that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was shortly after our meeting with the KLA where we suggested that they amnesty the two journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you ever learn whether there was any connection between your meeting and the release of these persons?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. The KLA was under a lot of pressure related to the case of these two journalists, and I am sure they heard from many quarters to release the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning to the next paragraph, that first sentence includes the phrase: "We wish to remind you of the discussions we had in Kosova, namely about the KLA's commitment to the rules of war." The discussions referred to here, which discussions are they that you are wishing to remind the recipients of?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Those are the discussions that took place in our meeting with Mr. Thaqi and Limaj in Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And maybe in the beginning, about the middle part of that paragraph: "We are well aware that the KLA's judicial structure are in the process of formation. However, this does not absolve you of your obligations under international law to provide humane treatment to detainees including a fair and open trial." Was this a reference also to your discussions during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. And our attempt here was to continue to engage in the dialogue with the KLA, to improve their conduct, and to actually implement their stated commitment to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And perhaps in furtherance to that, at the very last sentence of this letter you say: "We are" -- sorry. "We are particularly interested in continuing our discussions on the KLA's code of conduct for soldiers. And your cooperation with the War Crimes Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia." Did your discussions on either of those topics continue with the persons addressed in this letter?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I took no further part in those discussions and I cannot say whether we did have any more meetings with the KLA, especially not -- as far as I know, this is the only meeting we had with Thaqi and Limaj. We did continue our discussions with Mr. Demaqi and his role and his influence over KLA was relatively limited. And then a few months after this letter things just spun out of control in terms of the conflict and we were just completely overwhelmed documenting the vast level of abuses that was occurring in Kosova by the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: There are no further questions from the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. That's obviously a convenient time for the second break. We will resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, my name is Karim Khan, and I'm co-counsel representing Mr. Fatmir Limaj who sits behind me. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly requested to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You have to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Perhaps that's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: My last part of the introduction was that I think you have met Mr. Limaj on one occasion before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Hopefully, Mr. Bouckaert, I won't be too long with you, but I do have some important questions to ask. And I would be grateful if you take your time, don't rush, and answer, of course, carefully. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Because, of course, you understand that these are very important matters that you are speaking about.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I think you apologised to Mr. Limaj about not putting him down by name in a letter that you sent, and I can assure you that no offence at all was taken. Am I right also that you didn't intend to insult anyone at all, however inadvertent it may have been, when you recounted your humorous remark as you put it when you were leaving the meeting in which you said, "Now. If the KLA lost the war, they could open a zoo." I'm sure you didn't mean -- being a balanced individual, you didn't mean any offence by that, did you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. And I'm sorry if I did offend anybody by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know the meaning of the word "Celiku"?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It means steel, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, you of course have given evidence about reading a lot of material about Kosovo and the complex situation in the Balkans before you went to on your missions to that territory. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's normal to read up so that you are aware of the basic issues that may arise when you're seeking to discharge your mandate on behalf of Human Rights Watch. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You have been to Kosovo on two occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I have been to Kosovo since then also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: At the time of writing your reports you had been to Kosovo on two particular occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you say you had one meeting with -- for about two hours when you met Mr. Hashim Thaqi and my client, Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thats with an informal meeting, wasn't it, in an informal setting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you make any notes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We produced a summary of the content of the meeting about a week after for internal distribution at Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you had requested that meeting to discuss the matters that you have already outlined and you were granted that meeting. That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you say that Mr. Hashim Thaqi introduced himself as head of the political directorate. You have a clear recollection about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Isn't it right that my client in fact introduced himself to you as Commander Celiku?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: He introduced himself as Celiku, the head of the legal directorate of the general headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: See, it's that that I take issue with, so that you know, on behalf of my client. Do you know how Ram Buja was?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I know Rambouillet as a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In your -- in your studies of the KLA, had you ever heard of a commander called Ram Buja?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: How detailed in fact was your understanding of what departments or what individuals later on made up the General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: At that stage of our meeting, it was extremely limited. This was the first time that we had individuals identified as holding specific positions within the general headquarters of the KLA. Prior to that, we were only aware of some general spokespersons of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: See, in fact, -- and you don't speak Albanian, do you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And after your meeting in November 1998, it's correct to say that your colleague, Fred Abrahams, had various meetings with Mr. Limaj. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And are you aware that whenever Human Rights Watch asked for any assistance from Mr., Limaj whether during 1998 or thereafter, that is correct assistance was given by Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact, but we certainly had a very amicable meeting when I met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that towards the end of 1998 Mr. Limaj that did in fact become part of the General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. I only aware that he identified himself as such as our meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you herd of the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In all your research of Kosovo, your readings and travels speaking to Kosovans and members of the Serb humanitarian organisations and military you haven't heard about the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So it follows from that that you don't know who the head of the 121 Brigade was at the time that you met with Mr. Thaqi and my client.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You met in Banja?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I don't suppose you have any knowledge of where my client was born.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I believe he was born there Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: From your experience in going to different parts of Kosovo, is it correct that when you met with various individuals from the General Staff or from regional commanders, as you put them, that the local commander or the person in charge of that particular area would attend that meeting, as a courtesy. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that as a general principle, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it possible that you could be mistaken and what Mr. Limaj said was that he had studied law at Pristina University?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: He did say that at the meeting. But he did [Realtime transcript read in error: "didn't"] identify himself as head of the judicial directorate of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And in that capacity, you say, that he was in the General Staff, he was director of judicial matters in the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: General headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you -- please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The transcript, just to be clear, says on line 22, 23, the answer is he did say that at the meeting but he didn't identify himself as the judicial directorate. I believe the witness said "did," but perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer as I heard it was certainly that he did identify himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: From your very thorough investigations, your reading of papers and your meetings that you held on your two trips to Kosovo, have you ever heard from any other source that there was in fact at General Staff level somebody called director of judicial matters? Have you heard that from any other source apart from your recollection of what happened in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, you juxtaposed the attitude and willingness of Mr. Thaqi and Mr. Limaj at that meeting, as you put it, their will willingness to be open to a constructive dialogue to the attitude that you received from the Yugoslav authorities. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Absolutely. We had amicable and positive discussion with Mr. Thaqi and Limaj, at which they repeatedly said -- expressed their will willingness to adhere to Geneva Conventions and appeared to be cooperating quite willing Lee with our work, aside from the fact that they denied us the kind of details that we wanted. Which is not the kind of relationship that we enjoyed with the Yugoslav forces or officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And I think you said in effect there was no attempt, at least in relation to this, of any subterfuge by anybody at that meeting because Mr. Thaqi immediately interrupted you and immediately accepted that there were problems that happened in war.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We were less pleased with their responses when we asked for specific cases where they had addressed those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, of course, unfortunately, problems do happen in war, don't they?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In fact, problems happen even in very disciplined armies, don't they?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. The question is whether those problems are addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Even armies like -- in the United States Army, in the British army, in the Canadian army, even armies that have a very long and detailed tradition of military tactics and knowledge and rules of chivalry. even there, of course, problems happen in the heat of battle. That is a fair assessment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: As I have documented, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And from your meeting, in fact, there was no attempt to disguise that by anybody in that meeting. Problems did occur?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Certainly. As I pointed out previously, our main concern was how problems were addressed and we wanted the factual information about how KLA was addressing those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. The heart is willing, the body is infirm; you have heard that on mutilation, I suppose, of that saying before today, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't specifically recall hearing it, but I'm sure it's a saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, that that is the mercy on you, no doubt. But in these discussions, in fact a very real attempt was made to describe the difficulties that were facing the KLA as a fledging military organisation than was told to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We expressed very clearly in that meeting that we did not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. feel that these difficulties could justify summary executions and other abuses such as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bouckaert, I'm very aware of your position, of course, and it's also correct to say that Human Rights Watch has the very understandable and laudable aim to extend humanitarian law as widely as possible, to mitigate the ravages of war. I mean, that is the mandate of the Human Rights Watch. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I would disagree with you on that point. Our aim is to implement international humanitarian law, not necessarily to extend it. Because we feel that by extending international humanitarian law beyond its boundaries we actually end up undermining IHL. And the issue of -- the question of genocide in Darfur right now is a clear example. Human Rights Watch is not one of the organisations which has called situation in Darfur genocide because we want to have actual implementation of IHL, not necessarily extension of IHL.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it may be a bore, but going back just for the moment to Kosovo. It's correct, isn't it, that you described in your recollection Mr. Limaj talking about the attempts that were being made on the ground in the heat of battle to actually build something that could resemble civilian institutions that could implement international humanitarian of law and mitigate the ravages of war? I mean, that was being described to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, being a realist, knowing what it is like on the ground if war, of course, in conflict there are numerous different scenarios as to the state of organisation of the parties, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Ranging from tradition wars, as we have seen in Europe in the last 50 years, between two organised military structures, to guerrilla warfare, even where the state is not being evolved at all. I mean, between the two extremes, everything is possible?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And of course if an army has not previously existed, if there is, in effect, a largely spontaneous ground swell of support by a population to join a group, whether it's called a terrorist group or a resistance group, it will not be easy to immediately organise such a ground swell of popular support. There are difficulties, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: There could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In short, of course, you would accept that whatever the requirements on paper of IHL, or as far as implementing these objectives, different Armed Forces have to start somewhere?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. But the requirements and the tests for application of IHL are clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. But different Armed Forces have to start somewhere. They are not all at the same stage of evolution, are they?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, of course, even under, for example, Additional Protocol II you're quite aware that the law actually doesn't demand the impossible? It talks about the ability of the opposing party to implement the requirements of Additional Protocol II. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In fact, from your analysis and your study and your presence in Kosovo, it's correct to say on a balanced view that there were very major structural weaknesses in the Kosovo Liberation Army, even at the time that you went there in September. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I would be willing to say there were weaknesses. I wouldn't call them very major weaknesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Would you call them structural weaknesses, weaknesses of structure?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: There were some structural challenges that the KLA faced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, I think in your report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's tab 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You talk about instances. You say that seasoned war correspondents as well as Human Rights Watch researchers who encountered the UCK observed instances of discipline. This is in your report, isn't it? You instances of discipline were noted. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. But I object to the reading you're trying to give to that sentence. It does not suggest that in general there were -- there was indiscipline among the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And I also noted that there was no rigid hierarchical structure in the KLA in the period covered by this report from February to September. That's also accurate, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We're referring to the kind of military ranking that you would find in an organised army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You talk about separate internal factions?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Don't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course, in a regular army, a normal organised armed group, you don't get separate internal factions, do you, you get a clear chain of command. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I believe talking about the emergence of FARK, which was an organisation separate from UCK, but it remained very much a marginal player. Our report was issued at a time when this organisation had just emerged, but it did not become a very major player within the Kosovo conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'm not talking about FARK at the moment. I'm talking about internal factions not being present in normal -- in a normal military?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Where do you see the language "internal factions" in our description of UCK?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You say that there were internal factions during the period covered by this report?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you just tell me where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Top of page 92. "Although UCK is primarily a guerrilla army with no rigid hierarchical structure, and there are separate internal factions during the period covered by this report from February to September," and you then go on.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. FARK wasn't a part of the KLA, was it, it was a separate organisation?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was a breakaway faction would be proper way to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In answer to my question, that a normal army, regular army doesn't have internal factions, you would agree with me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We're talking about a guerrilla army, not a normal army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If could you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: A normal army typically would not have internal factions, although there are many armies which do have internal factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You talk about two journalists that had been detained and that was discussed in your meeting. You recollect that discussion?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Even individuals from very eminent organisations like Human Rights Watch were required to get a pass from Adem Demaqi in September 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We got a special pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No doubt very well deserved. But even from -- individuals from newspapers, journalists, they also required a pass from Adem Demaqi, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And at a roadblock, you would normally show the pass that had been issued. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And if an individual, if a journalist, if two journalists were stopped who did not have a pass, you don't think it would be unreasonable that they would be detained for further investigation?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I can't recall a single case where this happened with international journalists. It did happen that they were stopped at checkpoints and asked for a pass and turned back at those checkpoints, but I can't recall a single case where arrested and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The Tanjug newspaper you mentioned was sympathetic. I put it a mouthpiece of Slobodan Milosevic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I think I said in my testimony that we did not consider them an objective source all the time. And that they did have a pro-Yugoslav tendency in their reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You don't know, I suppose, what documents were found on those two journalists from that Belgrade newspaper?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. We were not provided with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But you do have evidence that they were released?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. They were amnestied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In fact, you don't have any evidence that those two journalists mistreated, do you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
