utterances.text: No. We never alleged they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You have no information, I'm not saying that you alleged it, but you have got no information at all as to how they were treated, the food they were given, and their conditions, the conditions that they were kept at during the time that they were detained by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We have no information to that extent because we were denied the KLA's permission to go visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course after these individuals were released, it was within your gift, within your decision, to go and meet these people?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You could have if you wanted?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you didn't?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, of course, having your ear to the ground, knowing what is going on, interacting with other agencies like the ICRC, UNHCR, newspapers, journalists, human rights organisations, you hear things that are germane to your work. That's fair isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: What do you mean by "germane"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You haven't heard anything after the release of these two journalists that would put you on notice to suspect that they were treated otherwise than in a dignified and decent manner; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, in your conversations with Mr. Thaqi I think you -- when it was being discussed about the difficulties of the KLA, the difficulties of organising in that time of strive, I think it's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Thaqi given an example of the Drenica zone. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't recall if it was Mr. Thaqi or Mr. Celiku, but they did discuss their attempts to put in place civilian structures in the Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And does it refresh your memory if in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: For my learned friends, it's paragraph 24 of the statement, the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Does it refresh your memory if I put to you that Mr. Thaqi explained they were in the process of setting up civilian structures in areas that they controlled giving the example of Drenica. Does that help you as to who said it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: At the moment I honestly don't recall if it was Mr. Thaqi or Mr. Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: From your--

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If questions will be put to him about the specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. But if there are going to be questions about statement, if he could please be shown them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: From your recollection of yours conversation, did you gain the impression that Drenica was being put forward as the perhaps the most -- the best example that Mr. Thaqi could offer as to whether the KLA was at the most advanced stage of evolution. Did you gain anything about that? Did you gain that impression or not?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't know if that is why the example was used. Drenica is a heavily Albanian populated area where the KLA was-- continued to have a presence even at the periods when the Yugoslav offensive was strongest. But I didn't gain that impression, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Generally in your meeting, and of course things are not perfect and always more can be done, but did you gain the impression from that meeting that what actually was being said to you is, Look, we know there are problems but we are trying our best to sort things out. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I do think that the meeting was very amicable and that the representatives we met with were serious about what they were saying, and they were serious when they said they were committed to the Geneva Conventions. However, we left the meeting less than pleased with their responses to some specific questions about the implementation of those stated commitments. So, in short, there was gap between their statements of intent and the actual examples they could provide us with showing that they were actually doing these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But individuals, those two individuals and perhaps two others were released very shortly after your meeting?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That's your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to thank Mr. Limaj again for the fact that those people were released, because there was a specific request during our meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You talk about massive violations committed the Yugoslav forces in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, these are detailed in your report that the Judges have so it's not my intention at all to belabour these issues. But you remember, do you, one particular incident in September 1998 when you went and saw a 18 month old child that had been killed. Do you remember what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Absolutely. The picture from that massacre is still on my desk today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Where was that it?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Was in Drenica, in Gornje Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what you saw?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We arrived there the day after Yugoslav forces moved through the village. They had found 18 members of the Limaj -- of the -- what is the name of the family?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Does the Obir [phoen] name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That is the name of the village, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I forget the name of the family we found 18 members of that family slaughtered in the forest, mostly women and children, most of them shot in the head and I spent most of time in spent and in November documenting that -- and other massacres which was the focus of our report, "A Week of Terror in Drenica: Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo".

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Was that the child that the Serbs had said was a doll?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: They said it a fake. It wasn't a real child it was just staging by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah. I have an entire chapter in "The Week of Terror" report which dealings with the response of the Yugoslav authorities which was absolutely ridiculous and dehumanising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It wasn't a doll?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't a doll, I saw the body myself and she wasn't the only child killed that day. There were two sisters of five and seven, I believe, who were also killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the circumstances of their death led you to what conclusions?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That they were executed in the forest by Yugoslav forces. They weren't even wearing their shoes. They had been sheltering and had been surprised by the Yugoslav forces and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't intend to go through all of these instances of Serb atrocities. They are in the papers that you've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I will be hopefully quite brief. Have you heard of Mr. Jan Kickert? He's a diplomat from Austria.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I knew him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: An experienced and capable diplomat, am I right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, he was a very courageous man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: There was a lot of propaganda in Kosovo 1998 and thereafter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Propaganda by whom? By the Yugoslav government, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, by all sides.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It happens in war?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. And it's part of your duties to separate propaganda from the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you talk about -- well, are you aware of allegations made by the Serb authorities of a mass burial site and a large-scale execution of women and children in Klecke?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, we investigated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It said that bodies burned in a kiln by the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Kickert's views were on that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't know what his views on them are. I know what our views were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You don't set much store by these allegations, do you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. We did not -- and if I can explain the reasons for that, the evidence that the Yugoslav forces presented to the international community were two ethnic Albanians whom they claimed were KLA members. Those people presented to media by a Serbian judge. I think her name was Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, we've hear her name before.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Who was a woman, I should say the so-called judge, because she was a woman who was deeply implicated in torture. People tortured in her presence. She had convicted people who were clearly the victims of torture. So we -- we cast serious doubt because of her role in this case, and the Yugoslav authorities never provided us with the kind of evidence we needed to actually confirm this case. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. And from your knowledge, perhaps gleaned either on the ground or from your following of reports afterwards, it's right, isn't it, that even the international forensic team that got involved, nobody has actually sustained any information, apart from the Serbs, of a mass execution site in Klecka committed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I would say that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did it seem to you, in fact, that that allegation was staged by the Serbs to dirty, to muddy the name of the KLA as part of the propaganda war. Would that be a reasonable assumption, sir?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We just were not able to confirm the allegations made by the Yugoslav government despite our best efforts, and this was a great source of frustration for us. I don't know if the case was staged or if we were simply unable to confirm the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say in your experience in Kosovo, your speaking to diplomats and all the rest, that the Serbs were not slow in making any allegation that they thought could show the KLA in the very worst possible light. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They certainly made a lot of allegation but when we went to them and asked for cooperation to confirm those allegations, we did not receive the kind of cooperation we needed to confirm those allegations. And in many case their own actions ended up destroying evidence of crimes which they claimed were committed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And of course in your experience from what you saw in Kosovo, if you -- if the Serbs actually had an example where there had been arbitrary killings by the KLA, you would expect them not to be shy about it, but to immediately bring to your attention?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This was our frustration actually even when there were cases when it appeared at least on a prima facie basis that they had evidence of KLA crimes such as it's bodies found in the lake near Glodjane, we did not receive the kind the cooperation we needed to substantiate those claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm not talking just yet about cooperation. I'm talking about actually telling you, These guys, the KLA, are a bad lot. Look what they've done. I'm not talking about evidence, I'm talking about allegation. It's right, isn't it, that they were not slow in making allegations?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, they published a white book on the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's right that in your time in Kosovo you never heard, even in September 1998, you never heard any allegations made by the Serbs against Celiku or Fatmir Limaj killing people in Lapusnik. You didn't hear that, did you?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such allegations personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Khan. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm so unused to using this thing. I will yield to Mr. Powles. It may be that I will have one or two questions, but it won't be more than that. I may not even have that, depending what Mr. Powles is going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I represent Mr. Isak Musliu who sits behind me. I hope that the matters I'm going to put to you are fairly uncontentious with the result that we should get through things fairly quickly; however, I doubt we will finish this evening leaving you with the prospect of having to spend the weekend in The Hague, and for that I apologise.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: There Three areas which I wish to consider with you. First of all, the aims and objectives of the KLA. Second of all, the structure of the KLA, to an extent, and then finally the context of what was going on in Kosovo in 1998, in particular, the activities of the Serb forces and authorities. So beginning, then, with the aims and objects of the KLA in particular in 1998, you, I think, testified -- you think, I testified, that the events in Drenica in February and March of 1998 really radicalised the ethnic Albanian population and caused a swelling in the ranks of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And really what happened in Drenica in February/March 1998 was the killing of 83 ethnic Albanians, including 24 women and children.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct. That case is documented in detail in our report, "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And it's the view of your colleague Mr. Fred Abrahams, when he testified in the Milosevic trial, that the Drenica massacres radicalised the Albania population and, in his words, "pushed them over the edge." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I wasn't present during the testimony. I think it's correct to say that it did radicalise the Albanian population, and caused massive upswelling of support for the KLA among the ethnic-Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Would you agree with his classification of it as having pushed people over the edge?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I would not have used those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Do you agree with his testimony that from that point, on it was clear a peaceful resolution to the conflict was no longer available?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I have, if counsel has it available, a reference to the Milosevic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Of course. It's page 6.062, perhaps in the early days of the Milosevic trial, 6.062, and I can give you a line reference as well. Yes, page 6.062, lines 24 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. In Mr. Abraham's words, in that trial, he said, "I believe he said I believe those incidents referring to Drenica were extremely important for the conflict because they radicalised the Albanian population. Up until that point, the KLA was still a disorganised and somewhat mysterious organisation. After the Drenica killings..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: "... I believe it was clear that a peaceful resolution to the conflict was no longer available." Would you agree with him that from that point on, a peaceful resolution to the conflict was no longer available?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I am a bit more of an optimist than Mr. Abrahams, I guess. I think a peaceful resolution to the conflict could always have been achieved, but it was an extremely remote possibility because of the actions of President Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. And it was those killings, in particular seeing the laughter of women and children that radicalised the Albanian population and caused them, in large numbers, to rise up and defend themselves. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't want you to put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Don't.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I will -- it led to a massive upsurge in support for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Of ordinary people rising to join the ranks of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, not everybody joined the KLA, but many -- mostly young and even some older old men did join the KLA at that stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: There were ordinary Kosovan Albanians, nothing special about them, ordinary folk.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, it drastically changed the situation in Kosovo, no doubt. And Adem Jashari became a martyr for the Albanian people, and in many, many Albanian houses we visited, his picture would be up on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. People who would perhaps rather not fight but perhaps felt compelled to do so, to defend themselves. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate on the reasons why people joined the KLA, whether to liberate Kosovo or to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Would you turn to tab 5 of the bundle of documents to pages 76 and 77, and we've already looked at these before. I, in particular, want to take you again to the quotations by Mr. Shaban Shala, a KLA commander, who used to be an activist with for the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms, and you include a lengthy quotation from him as to the actions of certain individuals within the KLA. And he said, as has already been presented to you by the Prosecution, that there were cases when individuals within the KLA made mistakes, this is on page 77, but as such, cases are punished by the KLA even if its soldiers conducted them.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. And again, it was our purpose to try to find documentation of these kind of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, he is accepting that individuals within KLA made have made mistakes, but if you look at the top of the quotation, he said this: "I can add in this context that the KLA general headquarters has not and will not issue an order to pursue, kill, or massacre innocent people or loot or destroy Serbian property." And then he laments, "However, not everything can be controlled during a war." Would you agree with his classification that it's -- it was not KLA policy to kill innocent people, or loot or destroy Serbian property. It may have happened at the hands of the individuals within the KLA but it wasn't one of their aims and objectives. Would you agree with that, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, we never saw any orders to the effect that -- issued by the general headquarters calling on their members to kill or massacre innocent people, or loot or destroy Serbian property.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree that it was one of the KLA's aims and objectives?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Moving on, then to the quotation from Adem Demaqi in interview with Radio B92, he stated the following: "When I talked to certain people from the headquarters, I saw that there united view on one thing, we do not deal in kidnappings. If some groups do it on their own and if we have influence on them, we always intervene and kidnapped persons are released. " Now, it very much seems that in his view, and in the KLA headquarters' view, there are some groups that will carry out some actions, namely kidnappings, on their on. Now, would you agree with that classification?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Whether it was groups that the kidnappings were being done by groups acting on their own?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: So you would not agree with a quotation of someone who you have included in your reports; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You disagree with a man who you've quoted?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We don't -- we quote the statement to -- to point to the fact that the KLA had repeatedly stated, publicly stated that they would abide by the Geneva Conventions. However, as I have repeatedly said, we had no evidence that they were actually punishing people, and it's a convenient excuse to use that the group is doing it on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Going back to your previous answer though, you stated that you had no evidence of a policy on the part of a KLA to carry out of murder of innocent people or loot or destroy Serbian property.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We said that -- I agree that there was no an order to pursue, kill, or massacre innocent people or loot and destroy Serbian property, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: But our concern was with the disciplinary procedures which were in place to address the kind of abuses that were clearly taking place in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Exactly. Leaving that to one side there may not have been such procedures in place, but you would agree that it was not KLA policy to be committed in the first place. Whether they addressed them thereafter was another matter?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I cannot agree -- I cannot testify that the KLA never issued an order to kill a particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Or a group of individuals. I can say that it wasn't their general policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't their general policy.

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: We'll move on, then, to perhaps what one of their general policies was and that was to protect the civilian population from Yugoslav forces. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I think we had a discussion in this in our report under orders. Many of the KLA attacks took place very close to Albanian civilian populations. And it was perfectly within the knowledge that the KLA would respond -- sorry, that the Yugoslav forces would respond with atrocities to those KLA attacks, including the case of Gornje Obrinje which we discussed earlier, where the young child was massacred and the KLA placed land-mines on the road just in front of that village, which killed a number of Yugoslav -- actually Serbian police soldiers. So in -- in that context, I -- I cannot agree with your statement. I think that the KLA at times endangered the civilian population through the kind of tactics it was using.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Are you seriously saying that the KLA did not at any time seek to protect the civilian population from the onslaught of Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that. But I'm saying that at the same time the KLA, through its military tactics, endangered that same civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Well, that may be your view --

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: And that's also the view expressed in our "Under Orders" report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Well, that may be your view, but would you also agree that at times the KLA undertook operations and actions to protect civilians from the onslaught of Serbian forces? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I'm certain there were such cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Do you know of any examples?

utterances.speaker: Peter BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I can't think of any off top of my head. In most of the massacres that I documented personally, there was no KLA presence in the villages, which only adds to the severity of abuses committed by the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour I see the time. It may be a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Powles. I'm sorry that it will be necessary to ask you to return on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will go and visit my relatives in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know it will cause you great heart rending, that. We will resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th of April, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
